## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- deploy-to-vercel: Deploy applications and websites to Vercel. Use when the user requests deployment actions like "deploy my app", "deploy and give me the link", "push this live", or "create a preview deployment".
- effective-go: Apply Go best practices, idioms, and conventions from golang.org/doc/effective_go. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring Go code to ensure idiomatic, clean, and efficient implementations.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- get-api-docs: Use this skill when you need documentation for a third-party library, SDK, or API before writing code that uses it — for example, "use the OpenAI API", "call the Stripe API", "use the Anthropic SDK", "query Pinecone", or any time the user asks you to write code against an external service and you need current API reference. Fetch the docs with chub before answering, rather than relying on training knowledge.
- merging-branches-safely: Use when asked to merge or rebase one branch into another, or when resuming an in-progress merge/rebase with unresolved conflicts. Covers `git merge`, `git rebase`, and cleanup after conflict aborts. Do not use for cherry-pick, push, or PR creation.
- rebasing-renovate-prs-locally: Use when manually rebasing a Renovate PR for a pnpm monorepo locally, instead of waiting for the Renovate workflow. Triggers on draining a Renovate PR backlog, paused Renovate cron, slow CI lockfile regeneration, or "rebase this Renovate PR now without spending Actions minutes."
- sweep-vercel-queue: Two-pass sweep of a Vercel team's QUEUED deployments. Pass 1 cancels ALL queued PREVIEW deployments by a given githubLogin (e.g. a CI bot firing a preview per project on every push). Pass 2 cancels queued PRODUCTION deployments by a given githubLogin, keeping the newest per project so the latest code still ships. Use for "sweep the Vercel queue", "drain queued previews", "cancel a bot's preview deploys", "cancel stale prod deploys keep latest per app". Both passes are opt-in via env/config.
- vercel-cli-with-tokens: Deploy and manage projects on Vercel using token-based authentication. Use when working with Vercel CLI using access tokens rather than interactive login — e.g. "deploy to vercel", "set up vercel", "add environment variables to vercel".
- vercel-composition-patterns: React composition patterns that scale. Use when refactoring components with boolean prop proliferation, building flexible component libraries, or designing reusable APIs. Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

content.thinking:
I'm seeing the core design tension now. The user's feedback has four straightforward items I can implement, but item 5 about the TOC footer creates a fundamental conflict—showing all phase names upfront in a clickable footer directly contradicts the current design philosophy of letting the tap reveal information progressively.

The bigger question is what happens to the verdict lines if the footer becomes a navigation element. Right now the tap both produces the verdict and advances, but if advancing becomes a footer click, the verdict needs a new home—it could appear after streaming finishes, become the phase description in the footer, or be dropped entirely. That choice fundamentally changes how the experience flows.

I'm also mapping out the actual phases: the state machine has five stages, but "offer" is transitional, so as a TOC it might be four distinct phases—continuation, question, dial, and flip—with the offer folding into the navigation action itself.

Clicking a phase should probably set up the whole demo configuration at once: switching the prompt, resetting the mode and console, and readying the Run button. That's a huge win for presentation flow. And then there's the question of whether the TOC shows all phases upfront, spoiling the journey, or reveals them progressively—but given the need to jump between phases, I think all labels should be visible from the start, even if the controls themselves stay hidden until reached.

For the temperature control, the issue is that it vanishes when toggling post-trained, which feels disconnected. I'm weighing whether to keep it persistent across modes or relocate it somewhere more stable.

The cleanest approach is to leave the dial in place but dim it to about 40% opacity with a visual "flattened" indicator when post-trained activates—this preserves the layout and keeps the visual argument intact without the jarring disappearance.

For the model name itself, I'm restructuring the chrome so "davinci-002" stays as the persistent base, with the mode toggle appearing right next to it as `[base | post-trained]` rather than replacing the nameplate entirely.

On the spacing question, I can reserve the switch's area from the start so there's no layout shift when it appears—and when the switch shows up, I'll drop the "· base" suffix from the initial nameplate since the toggle now makes that explicit.

For the tabs, I'm treating the prompt selector as visually connected tabs that sit directly on top of the generation window, sharing its border styling so the active tab blends seamlessly into the content area below.

At the initial state, showing just one tab ("a half-written function") feels more natural than hiding the entire strip—it labels the window without spoiling what's coming, then the second tab materializes. That's cleaner than the whole selector suddenly appearing.

On height stability, I need to reserve enough vertical space in the pre-block to accommodate the longest completion across all scenarios—the reverse-function case runs about five lines total, so I'll set a fixed height that handles that without causing reflow. The verdict and footer regions need reserved space too to prevent shifting. If the offer strip gets folded into the TOC as a phase, it could disappear entirely and the theatrical moment becomes the phase label instead — that eliminates a whole layout shift. Alternatively, the offer could live in a permanently allocated slot below the console, or become a labeled "next" arrow in the footer, though that wastes space either way. I'm trying to figure out what to prioritize asking about, since the skill constraint is one question at a time but that feels slow given the complexity. I'm realizing the TOC actually replaces the gating mechanism entirely—clicking a phase sets the stage to that number, and gates become a monotone maximum. That's the foundational shift. Now I need to ask the key question: who delivers the verdict now that the tap no longer does both speaking and advancing?

content.text:
I've read the demo, its stage machine, verdicts, chrome, and the stepper it borrows its visual grammar from. Your four directive items I can design without asking. The footer change is the one that moves load-bearing walls, so let me start there.

The verdict tap was doing **two jobs**: it advanced the stage, *and* it was the thing that let the page speak only after you'd spoken. A TOC footer takes over "advance" cleanly. But that leaves the verdict lines — *"It didn't answer — it just kept going. There's no one in there to ask."* — without a trigger.

**Who speaks them now?**

**(a) The page speaks, late and quiet.** The verdict fades in ~1.5s after the stream finishes, in the muted italic, in a slot that's always reserved so nothing moves. This is option (a) from our first round, which you passed over — but the objection then was that the page beats you to the line, and a deliberate delay plus your own pacing mostly answers that. Zero extra clicks, which is what you just asked for.

**(b) The verdict becomes the phase's own text, in the footer.** Each TOC entry has a short label (`it completes`) and, when it's the *current* phase and a run has finished, the full line renders beside or under the strip. The footer stops being just navigation and becomes the demo's narrator-of-record. One less region on screen, and the line is anchored to the beat rather than to the run.

**(c) Verdicts move out of the demo entirely** — into the era prose above it, as static text the audience can read cold. The demo goes silent and becomes pure instrument. Cleanest layout, but the cold-link reader loses the "no one is home" punch at the moment it lands.

content.thinking: The real question is whether the table of contents should display all phases upfront or unfold them as the user progresses through the content. This matters because it directly conflicts with his requirement to avoid spoiling information he hasn't reached yet.

content.text:
Locked: the page speaks, late and quiet, into a slot that's always there.

Next: **what the footer shows before you've reached it.**

Your founding constraint was *"I'd prefer not to display things I haven't gotten to yet — if I start with the base model, the audience doesn't know I'm going to talk about instruct post-training."* A table of contents is, by definition, the list of things you haven't gotten to. So one of the two has to bend.

**(a) Full TOC from the first second.** All five entries named and clickable: `it completes` · `no one answers` · `the dice` · `2022` · `it answers`. Honest, instantly legible, and every jump is one click. But `it answers` sits on the projector from minute one, and the room can read ahead of you. The ChatGPT-moment reveal becomes a thing they were waiting for rather than a thing that happened.

**(b) Progressive TOC — reached phases named, future phases as dim unnamed slots.** The strip is full-width and full-count from the start (so no layout shift, ever), but unreached entries render as `·····` or a muted number in the same footprint. They're still clickable — that's your fumble escape and your jump-ahead — they just don't tell the room what's coming. Each label writes itself in as you arrive.

**(c) Two-layer: audience TOC and presenter TOC.** Named for you, dots for them. Requires a second display or a mode toggle — which you already rejected once, for good reason.

My call is **(b)**. It's the only one that gives you the transport you asked for without handing the room your ending. The unnamed slot is also a small piece of theatre on its own: five stations, and the machine tells you what each one was only once you've stood on it. And it costs nothing structurally — the footer is one fixed-height row either way; the only difference is whether a label renders or a placeholder does.

Where I'd push back on myself: for the cold reader opening the link next month with nobody narrating, dots are less inviting than labels. I'd fix that by having the labels fill in *permanently* once reached, and by not resetting on step navigation — so anyone who walks the demo once has a full TOC from then on.

(b), or does the room reading ahead not actually bother you?

There's a significant pivot happening here: introducing a presenter mode toggle that fundamentally changes how the interface behaves. Without it, everything displays at once with no phased disclosure. With it enabled, the staged console and TOC footer appear. It's interesting that Eric initially rejected presenter mode for verdicts because it added cognitive overhead in high-pressure moments, but now he's reconsidering it as a way to gate the entire staged disclosure system rather than just muting certain elements.

The practical solution to his earlier concern is using a URL parameter — a presenter can bookmark the `?presenter=1` link and avoid any last-minute clicks or memory load. This also keeps the audience-facing URL clean and simple. The mode should be global across the whole masterclass page since there are multiple demos, though only Era I will use it initially. In default view, all controls stay visible (nameplate, switch, both tabs, dial) with no TOC footer, and the verdict still appears after a run as part of the cold reader's narration. The offer strip gets cut since it's meaningless without phases. The other options each have drawbacks — a visible control clutters the interface and risks audience confusion, a keyboard shortcut is premature since global shortcuts aren't solved yet, and localStorage persistence is risky on borrowed devices. URL params solve his original concern cleanly: the mode lives in the link itself, not in memory, and once keyboard shortcuts are ready, they can toggle it live without any other changes needed. I'll go with that recommendation.

content.text:
That's a better resolution than the one I argued for — and it retires my own earlier objection to presenter mode. When I called it "a second mode to remember at 19:00," it was going to control *page voice*, so forgetting it meant the page talking over you all night. Controlling *disclosure* is different: forget it and you get the site's normal view, which is a perfectly good demo. The failure mode is mild instead of embarrassing.

So: **how do you enter it?**

**(a) URL parameter — `?presenter=1`, alongside the `?step=` you already have.** You bookmark the presenter link; the audience gets the bare one. Nothing on screen, nothing to remember at 19:00 — you open the bookmark you always open. Survives reload, which matters if the projector hiccups. It can't be flipped mid-talk without touching the URL bar, but I don't think you ever want to.

**(b) A control in the page chrome** — a small toggle in the stepper header. Flippable live, but it's visible to the room, it's one more thing on the projector, and a site visitor can turn it on and land in a half-empty demo wondering what broke.

**(c) A key chord — `Shift+P`.** Invisible and live-flippable, but you just told me global keyboard shortcuts are the unsolved problem you want to tackle first. Building this on top of that would be building on the thing you flagged as not-yet-load-bearing.

My call is **(a)**, and I'd add: read it once at mount, don't persist it to localStorage. Sticky presenter mode is a trap — you demo on a borrowed laptop or someone opens your bookmark, and now the mode outlives the room it was for. The URL is the memory.

When global shortcuts land, (c) becomes a live toggle on top of the same flag, with nothing else changing.

Two things I'm treating as settled unless you say otherwise:

- **The flag is page-global, Era I is just its first consumer.** It'll be read at the masterclass page level and passed down, so Era II–IV demos can opt into staged disclosure later without re-litigating how the mode works.
- **Default mode shows everything and keeps the verdicts.** Full chrome — `davinci-002` with both switch positions, both prompt tabs, the dial — no TOC footer, no `2022 · humans taught it a format` offer strip (that strip is a beat, and there are no beats). The verdict still fades in quietly after each run, because that's exactly the narration the cold reader needs.

Does (a) hold, and do those two reads match what you meant by "everything is there, no phases"?

Let me verify there are no conflicts with the existing global arrow-key listener and make sure Shift+P won't interfere with the slider's arrow key handling—it should be safe since there are no text inputs. I'll check the masterclass.tsx file to see what key handlers are already in place before moving forward with the design.

Since `stepKeyDirection` already filters out modified keys, Shift+P won't interfere with arrow navigation, so I can add a separate `isPresenterToggle` predicate function in the same file. I'll present the design in sections and get approval as I go, starting with how the presenter flag works via a query parameter using `parseAsBoolean` from nuqs.

The key detail: use `history: "replace"` for the presenter toggle so it doesn't pollute the browser back stack the way step navigation does with "push". For the keyboard shortcut itself, Shift+P should toggle the presenter mode, guarded by checks for modifier keys, repeat events, and whether the event was already handled. The tricky part is deciding which targets should block the toggle — I need to exclude text entry fields like inputs and textareas, but sliders shouldn't block it since typing P while focused on a slider should still work. So I'll create a narrower `isTextEntryTarget` selector instead of reusing the broader arrow-consuming target check.

The presenter flag gets passed down as a prop from `Masterclass` to `Era1Playground` — one consumer doesn't need context, and a prop from the page component is page-global enough for future extensibility.

Now for the UI logic: instead of branching on presenter mode everywhere, I'm defining a single `Disposition` interface that derives what should display based on the presenter flag and current stage. This consolidates all the visibility rules — mode switch, dial, secondary prompt, footer TOC, offer — into one place. I'll add this to `stage.ts` since it's already small and owns the logic for what appears on screen.

For the phases and footer navigation, I'm reconsidering whether "offer" stays as a distinct stage or becomes a phase within the TOC. The current flow is continuation → question → dial → offer → flip, where offer shows a dashed strip. With a table of contents, clicking a phase needs to map cleanly to the stage machine.

The offer's only interactive element was a button advancing to flip, so it's functionally redundant as a phase. But it carries narrative weight — "2022 · humans taught it a format" is a real historical beat. I could keep it as a phase whose content becomes the TOC label plus a console line, though that leaves phase 4 without interaction. Or I fold it entirely: make phase 4 "it answers" (the flip state), and let the morph plus auto-run happen on arrival, with the historical caption appearing as chrome next to the switch. That gives me four clean phases with the narrative moment preserved but integrated differently.

The auto-run on phase 4 is actually good — he liked it. Landing there triggers mode→instruct, prompt→question, and runs automatically. One click, done. The risk of re-running if the presenter steps back and forth is fine. But stepping backward from phase 4 to phase 3 needs to reverse the state: mode→base, dial back to its original position.

Each phase arrival clears the console and reconfigures the machine, which means navigating back and forth will wipe what's on screen — that's correct behavior for a transport. The asymmetry matters though: phases 1–3 configure and clear but wait for a manual Run (you talk first, then run), while phase 4 auto-runs because the flip itself is the moment. That distinction is defensible and already agreed upon, but it's worth remembering on stage.

The footer in presenter mode shows reached phases with their labels and unreached ones as fixed-width placeholders to prevent horizontal reflow when labels appear. I'm using the same flex-1 equal-width cell structure as the stepper header, with an underline on the active phase and a cyan bottom border to match the design system.

I'm considering whether having two underline-based navigators—one at the page level for eras and one at the demo level for beats—might be confusing, but the visual context should distinguish them: the demo footer sits inside the console border in smaller monospace type with numbers, while the stepper sits outside in sans serif without numbers. The parallel actually reinforces the pattern of "underline means current position" at both levels.

Navigation arrows appear at the ends and disable at the boundaries, and I'm working through whether clicking an unreached phase jumps directly to it.

Now I'm laying out the chrome—the fixed header row with the model name, a switch for base versus post-trained, and temperature control. The model name stays constant, and the switch occupies a fixed slot, though before presenter mode kicks in it might just show a static label in the same space.

The key insight is that `davinci-002` never moves, but the switch morphs from a text suffix into a two-cell toggle. To avoid layout jank, I'll reserve the full switch width from the start, then fade in the `post-trained` cell once it's needed. That way the container grows rightward smoothly without any jarring shifts.

For temperature, it should appear at phase 3 in presenter mode and stay visible, but when the model switches to post-trained, it becomes inert — dimmed, disabled, with the readout replaced by a struck-through dash and a tooltip explaining that post-training flattened the temperature control.

I'm noticing the feedback about temperature feeling misplaced could mean either that it shouldn't disappear or that its position is wrong. Rather than ask again, I'll present my interpretation — keeping it in place but inert — as part of the design and invite correction during review.

For the default mode, everything displays without any hidden reveals or layout shifts. Now moving to the prompt tabs section, I'm designing the active tab to share the output panel's background with borders on three sides, while inactive tabs stay muted with their bottom border visible as part of the panel edge. Since tabs make the "prompt" label redundant, I'll remove it to clean up the interface.

In the first phase, only one tab shows initially with the second fading in as needed. The tabs expand horizontally into empty space without any vertical movement. For accessibility, I'm using proper ARIA roles like `role="tablist"` and `role="tab"` with `aria-selected`, but there's a complication — adding these roles would trigger arrow-key consumption in the selector without actually implementing tab navigation, which would be a regression. I need to either implement roving-tabindex arrow navigation or find another approach.

Given that keyboard navigation isn't a priority yet and there are other keyboard concerns to solve first, I'll go with plain buttons styled as tabs using `aria-pressed` instead. This avoids promising ARIA semantics we don't support and prevents silently swallowing arrow keys. The footer TOC can follow the same pattern with `aria-current`, keeping it consistent with how the stepper header works.

For layout stability, I'm fixing the output container to a specific height rather than using min-height, sized to accommodate the longest possible content. Counting line breaks across the different prompt variations to find the actual maximum—the reverse-fn prefix with high continuation hits 6 lines, the low variant goes up to 7 or 8 depending on trailing newlines, and the how-do-i prefix is starting its count with the instructAnswer section spanning multiple lines with blank lines between code blocks.

For the layout, I'm settling on a fixed height of around 256 pixels for the console output area with overflow scrolling on narrow screens, which trades off some empty space at the start for keeping the Run button stable. The verdict slot will also be fixed height for consistency, sized to fit about 2 lines of smaller text.

For the chrome, I'm letting the dial fade in at phase 3 without reserving its width upfront — since it only shifts horizontally within the chrome itself and doesn't affect anything below, I can position it to grow rightward with `ml-auto` on the reset button, so nothing jumps vertically when it appears.

The offer strip is being removed entirely, with its content folded into the phase-4 label. For the temperature whisper, I'm reconsidering whether to keep it as a separate row (which causes vertical shifts) or integrate it elsewhere — maybe as a caption under the dial in the chrome, though that changes the chrome's height, or as part of the phase-3 description in the footer TOC, but the footer cells are too narrow for that.

The cleanest approach: eliminate the separate whisper row and use the verdict slot itself as a single-line console that displays either the phase's whisper text when entering phase 3 (before any run) or the actual verdict after the run completes. This consolidates everything into one fixed slot with no new geometry, and in default mode (no phases) it simply shows verdicts only.

For mode persistence, I'm extending the session store to capture the entire resumable state — stage, mode, promptId, and temperature — so stepping away and returning keeps everything intact. Storing the full text on completion and preserving what's shown if navigating away mid-stream means returning to a finished run. For the code structure, I'm deciding whether to keep the presenter toggle logic in `step-keys.ts` or rename the file to something broader like `keys.ts` to reflect its growing scope—I'll stick with the current name and just add the function to avoid churn.

For the new modules, I'm setting up `disposition.ts` to compute presenter/stage/mode combinations, `phases.ts` to manage the phase list with labels and config mappings, and updating `stage.ts` to remove the `offer` stage, which cascades into test changes and affects the advance logic.

The big shift is that in presenter mode, advancement no longer happens through run verdicts—it's purely footer-driven. That means the gate logic checking question mode and band constraints disappears entirely, and `advance()` simplifies to just tracking the maximum reached stage. This actually collapses `stage.ts` into `phases.ts` since both are now just an ordered list with a `reached()` check.

I'm losing the gates' disciplinary function—they forced you to actually complete each step before unlocking the next control. But the presenter mode trades that for explicit TOC navigation, which is what was requested. It's a fair tradeoff for reducing the cognitive load.

The new component structure is: a nameplate constant and single-cell growing switch in the console chrome, a new tab strip for phase selection, a new footer with the TOC and navigation arrows, plus the session store capturing full snapshots and verdicts staying unchanged. I'm deleting `stage.ts` and its test suite since phases now handles everything.

Reconsidering the four phases and their captions—phase 4 auto-runs, so any caption gets immediately replaced by the verdict. Instead, I'll add a sublabel to the footer cell (like the stepper's vibe line) to show "2022 · humans taught it a format" when post-training is active. a sub-line showing only `2022` for phase 4 while keeping the other cells with reserved space for alignment. Now I'm moving on to write up the design presentation itself, organizing it into sections and asking for line-by-line feedback like before.

content.text:
I have what I need. Here's the design — six sections, veto any line.

---

## 1 · The presenter flag

`?presenter=1` via nuqs, alongside `?step=`, but with `history: "replace"` — otherwise every toggle lands in the back stack and your ← arrow starts undoing presenter mode instead of stepping eras.

`Shift+P` toggles it live. It goes in `step-keys.ts` as a sibling pure predicate to `stepKeyDirection`, and it's already safe by construction: that function rejects any modified key, so the arrow nav can't see it. Its own guard is narrower than the arrow guard — arrows must yield to sliders and tabs, but `P` only needs to yield to genuine text entry (`input`, `textarea`, `contenteditable`), of which this page currently has none.

The flag is read once in `masterclass.tsx` and passed to `<Era1Playground presenter={presenter} />` as a prop. No context — one consumer today, and a prop is the honest interface when Era II wants one.

## 2 · Two dispositions, one console

There is no second code path. A pure `dispositionFor({ presenter, stage, mode })` returns the six booleans the console reads:

| | default | presenter |
|---|---|---|
| mode switch | both cells | `base` only until phase 4 |
| second prompt tab | yes | from phase 2 |
| dial | yes | from phase 3 |
| dial live | `mode === "base"` | `mode === "base"` |
| footer TOC | **no** | yes |

That table is the whole difference. It lives in one tested file so `presenter ? … : …` never appears in JSX.

## 3 · Four phases, and what the footer is

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ←    ① it completes   ② no one answers   ③ ·····   ④ ·····   → │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Equal-width cells, `flex-1`, cyan underline on the current one — deliberately the stepper header's grammar, one altitude down, so it costs the room no new vocabulary. Numbered and mono and *inside* the console border, so it doesn't read as a second era-stepper.

Unreached phases render `·····` in a reserved two-line cell. Clicking one jumps there and reveals everything up to it. Labels, once written in, stay written for the session.

| # | label | sub-line | arriving sets |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `it completes` | | function prompt, base, 0.7 |
| 2 | `no one answers` | | question prompt, base |
| 3 | `the dice` | | question prompt, base, dial live |
| 4 | `it answers` | `2022` | question prompt, **post-trained**, auto-runs |

**The offer strip is deleted.** `2022 · humans taught it a format` becomes phase 4's sub-line, and the sentence itself already lives in the verdict you get on arrival — *"…because humans taught it the format. That flip is the ChatGPT moment."* One less region, one less thing that appears and shoves the page down.

**Two consequences I want you to see clearly:**

- **Arriving at a phase clears the output.** It's a transport; stepping ⟵ from 4 to 3 puts the base machine back with an empty console, ready to Run. Phases 1–3 wait for you to Run. Phase 4 auto-runs, because the flip *is* the moment. That asymmetry is one thing to hold on stage; I think it's the right one, but it is a thing.
- **All the gate logic dies.** Today the machine won't open the dial unless you actually ran the question in base, and won't open the offer unless you actually moved the dial. Those gates enforced the discipline the footer now hands to you. That's 12 tests deleted and `stage.ts` collapsing into a plain ordered `phases.ts`. It's what you asked for — I just want it said out loud rather than discovered later.

## 4 · The chrome

```
davinci-002  [ base ][ post-trained ]      temp ──●── 0.7 steady        ↺
             └─ fixed-width slot ─┘        └─ reserved from the start ─┘
```

`davinci-002` never moves and never changes. The switch is **present from the first second with one cell** — a one-position switch, which reads as a nameplate — and `post-trained` fades into the slot beside it. That's not a morph at all, so item 3 dissolves: there's nothing to crossfade, just a cell arriving. The slot is sized for two cells from the start, so nothing to its right ever shifts.

The dial's slot is reserved the same way — a fixed-width gap in the instrument panel until phase 3, then the slider fades into it.

**Temperature stops disappearing.** Once it's there it stays there. When the switch says `post-trained` it goes inert in place: dimmed, `disabled`, thumb parked, readout replaced by `—`. The argument that post-training flattened the dice is now *shown* rather than made by absence — which I think is what you meant by "misplaced." If you meant its *position* is wrong rather than its vanishing, say so and I'll move it.

## 5 · Prompt tabs, and the one line the console speaks

```
┌─────────────────────┬────────────┐
│ a half-written fn   │ a question │   active tab shares the panel's fill,
├─────────────────────┴────────────┴───────────────────┐   its bottom edge open
│ function reverseList(items) {                        │
│   return items.slice().reverse();                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The `PROMPT` eyebrow goes away — a tab strip doesn't need to announce it's a tab strip, and that's one of the 11px labels gone. In presenter mode phase 1 has a single tab; the second grows in rightward, so the growth is horizontal and nothing below moves.

These are plain buttons with `aria-pressed`, **not** `role="tab"`. `role="tab"` is in the arrow-consuming selector, so adopting it would silently swallow → on a focused tab with nothing implementing roving focus — a live regression for the sake of correct-looking ARIA. It becomes real tabs when you do the in-demo keyboard pass.

One fixed slot under the output that shows either the phase's line or the run's line, always the same height, never empty of reserved space.

## 6 · Nothing moves

Five concrete measures. The one that costs something:

**The output panel gets a fixed height, not `min-h-40`.** Sized to the tallest prefix + completion across every prompt × band × mode — a constant with a test asserting no combination exceeds it, so adding copy later fails loudly instead of reintroducing the jump. That's about 8 lines at `leading-7`, ~16rem. At phase 1, with two lines loaded, that's a visibly empty console. **That emptiness is the price of the Run button never moving,** and on a projector I think a machine with a big blank screen reads fine — but it's the one place where fixing your complaint has a real aesthetic cost, so it's your call, not mine.

The rest are free: fixed chrome row height, reserved switch and dial slots, the always-present verdict slot, and the offer strip and whisper row deleted rather than animated.

**Session store** grows from one field to the whole snapshot — `stage`, `mode`, `promptId`, `temp`, `output`, `verdict` — so "keep the state wherever it's at" means exactly that: step to Era II and back and the screen is identical, mid-demo, output and all. A run in flight is stored as its finished text rather than frozen mid-stream. Page reload still starts fresh; `↺` still re-arms deliberately.

So the dial genuinely has no effect, which is why keeping it inert is the honest approach that reflects how the system actually works.

But there's a stronger argument for making it live: I could author three instruct answers per temperature band (low, mid, high), making the data structure symmetric with the base mode. This way the dial works in both modes and demonstrates something more truthful—that temperature still exists post-training, it just doesn't break the format. The narrative becomes more powerful: crank the temperature up in base mode and you get gibberish, but crank it up post-training and you still get coherent answers, just chattier. That's a better teaching point about what post-training actually accomplishes. The cost is six new completions to replace the two static `instructAnswer` fields, but it eliminates the inert state entirely and keeps the layout perfectly stable.

For the footer accordion, I'm thinking about how to handle the collapsed state. The active phase shows its full label while the others collapse to just their numbers, still clickable. With equal-width flex cells, collapsing to numbers alone wastes space, so the accordion should actually resize the cells—the active one expands to fit its label while the others shrink down. Good — three of those tighten it. Taking them in order.

## 2 · The dial in post-trained

Honest answer: because the *data* has no dice on that side. `selectCompletion` returns a single `instructAnswer` per prompt regardless of band, so in post-trained the slider is a control wired to nothing. Retracting it (the old design) and dimming it (my proposal) are both dressings on that same hole.

Which means your question is really a design question, and the better answer is **fill the hole**: author instruct completions per band, same shape as `continuations`. Then the dial is simply always live once revealed — no dimming, no `—`, no rule to remember, no state to keep true.

And it's a *better* beat than the one it replaces. Right now the argument is "post-training took the dice away," which is both a bit false and made by absence. With a live dial you get to do this on stage: crank to 1.4 in base → it asks *how do I reverse time? who is asking?*. Flip to post-trained, same 1.4, don't touch anything → it still answers the question. Chattier, looser, maybe a stray aside, but the format holds. **The dice are still there. The format just doesn't care.** That's the truer claim about what post-training did, and it's the one your seniors will nod at — ChatGPT has a temperature too.

Cost is four strings (2 prompts × low/mid/high, minus the two that already exist as the mid case) and one extra verdict line for the high-band instruct run. `verdictFor` already keys on band, so it's a new constant, not new machinery.

## 3 · The footer as an accordion

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ←   ①   ②  no one home   ③   ④                              → │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Only the current cell carries its label; the rest are numerals, still clickable. Cells animate their width, so the motion is horizontal, in the last row, with nothing below it to shove — layout-stable in the sense you care about.

This also retires the whole progressive-reveal argument from two rounds ago. Collapsed cells are bare numerals, so nothing is spoiled *regardless* of how revealing the labels are, and the dot placeholders were only ever solving that. One less concept.

**Labels.** Four sets, different registers:

| | A · what it does | **B · the exhibit** | C · plain | D · your cue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ① | it continues | **the pattern** | autocomplete | finish the function |
| ② | it doesn't answer | **no one home** | nobody answers | ask it something |
| ③ | it rolls dice | **the dice** | randomness | turn the dial |
| ④ | it answers | **2022 · the format** | taught to answer | load the format |

I'd take **B**. Four nouns, each a thing you can point at — museum placards, not stage directions. They map 1:1 onto the four sentences you actually say, and `no one home` is already your own verdict line coming back as a title. A directs the room slightly (it's narrating for you); C is the most legible to a non-technical room and the least characterful; D is genuinely useful as a glance-down memory aid but it's the page telling the room what's about to happen, which is the thing you hired me not to do.

The `2022` rides inline on ④ only. Repeating `2019` on the first three is noise — the date matters on exactly one beat, because that beat *is* a date.

## Phase 4 waits

Agreed, and it makes the phases fully symmetric: **every** phase configures the machine and stops. Arriving at ④ sets post-trained, loads the question, clears the console, and sits there until you press Run. The asymmetry I flagged is gone, which is a straight improvement.

My read of "navigation should not start any animations": no run ever begins on its own, and nothing streams. Controls arriving still fade in over 250ms — a fade is the opposite of a jump, and you approved it for the verdict. Say the word if you meant those too and I'll make reveals instant.

---

Everything else stands as written: fixed-height output panel, gates deleted, `?presenter=1` + `Shift+P`, tabs joined to the panel, whisper and offer strip folded away, full-snapshot session store.

Three yes/nos and I'll write the spec: **live dial in post-trained with per-band instruct answers**, **label set B**, and **fades-on-reveal stay**.

# Masterclass — Design Update: Era I Presenter Transport

**Date:** 2026-07-25 · **Supersedes:** `2026-07-24-masterclass-era1-staged-console-design.md` · **Event:** 2026-07-28

The staged console shipped and was walked live. Four things came back from that
walk, and one of them moves a load-bearing wall.

**The transport is too much work.** Every beat costs a tap on `↩ what just
happened` before the next control appears. On stage that reads as leg work — the
presenter clicking his way forward rather than talking.

**The layout jumps.** Controls arrive, the whisper row leaves, the offer strip
appears, and the output panel grows with its own content — so the `Run` button
moves while the room is watching the output. Eric loses his own focus on what
changed.

**The chrome loses its identity.** `davinci-002` is replaced by the switch rather
than joined by it, and the temperature dial vanishes when post-trained loads.

**Progressive disclosure is wrong for the web.** It serves the room on the night
and punishes everyone who opens the link afterwards.

This redesign replaces the verdict-tap transport with a **presenter mode plus a
phase footer**, and makes the console geometrically fixed.

## 1 · Presenter mode

Progressive disclosure becomes opt-in rather than universal.

- **Default (no flag).** Everything is on screen: both switch positions, both
  prompt tabs, the dial. No phase footer. This is what a visitor gets from a
  shared link, and it is a complete demo — nothing to click your way through.
- **Presenter mode.** The console reveals itself one phase at a time, driven by
  the footer.

**Entry is `?presenter=1`**, read via `nuqs` in `masterclass.tsx` alongside the
existing `?step=`, with `history: "replace"`. Push history would put every toggle
in the back stack, so the global `←` arrow would start undoing presenter mode
instead of stepping eras.

**`Shift+P` toggles it live.** This is safe against the existing arrow-key
navigation by construction: `stepKeyDirection` already returns `null` for any
modified key, so it cannot see `Shift+P`. The new predicate's own guard is
narrower than the arrow guard — arrows must yield to sliders, tabs and radios,
but `P` only needs to yield to genuine text entry (`input`, `textarea`,
`[contenteditable]`), of which this page currently has none.

The flag is read once at the page level and passed to `<Era1Playground
presenter />` as a prop. No React context: one consumer today, and a prop is the
honest interface when Era II wants one.

**Not persisted to `localStorage`.** Sticky presenter mode is a trap — demo on a
borrowed laptop, or hand someone your bookmark, and the mode outlives the room it
was for. The URL is the memory.

### Why presenter mode retires the earlier objection

The 2026-07-24 conversation rejected a presenter mode because it was going to
control *page voice*: forget the toggle and the page narrates over you all
evening. Controlling *disclosure* inverts the failure mode. Forget the flag and
you get the site's normal view — a perfectly good demo, fully populated. Mild
instead of embarrassing.

## 2 · One disposition, no branching

There is no second code path for the two modes. A pure
`dispositionFor({ presenter, phase, reached })` returns the flags the console
reads, and it is the single place the two modes reconcile so that
`presenter ? … : …` never appears in JSX.

| | default | presenter |
|---|---|---|
| `post-trained` switch cell | present | from phase 4 |
| second prompt tab | present | from phase 2 |
| temperature dial | present | from phase 3 |
| phase footer | absent | present |
| `↺` reset | present | present |

**Disclosure follows `reached`, not `phase`.** Gates remain monotone: jumping
back to phase 1 after reaching 4 highlights phase 1 in the footer but does not
take the dial away. Closing gates would make the footer a trap — step back to
check something and lose the control you were about to use.

## 3 · The phase footer

Presenter mode only. A single fixed-height row inside the console's bottom
border.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ←   ①   ②  nobody answers   ③   ④                           → │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Accordion, one open at a time.** Only the current phase carries its label; the
rest collapse to bare numerals. Every numeral stays clickable, so a jump forward
or back is always one click. `←` / `→` step by one and disable at the bounds.

Cells animate their width. The motion is horizontal, in the last row of the
console, with nothing below it — layout-stable in the sense that matters.

**The accordion also retires progressive labelling.** An earlier draft used
`·····` placeholders so unreached phase names couldn't spoil the ending. Collapsed
cells are bare numerals regardless of how far you've got, so nothing is spoiled
and the placeholder concept disappears.

| # | label | on arrival |
|---|---|---|
| ① | `autocomplete` | function prompt, base, temp → 0.7 |
| ② | `nobody answers` | question prompt, base, temp → 0.7 |
| ③ | `turn the dial` | question prompt, base, temp → 0.7, dial revealed |
| ④ | `2022 · taught to answer` | question prompt, post-trained, **temp untouched** |

The `2022` rides inline on ④ alone. Repeating `2019` across the first three is
noise; the date matters on exactly one beat, because that beat *is* a date.

**Every phase configures the machine and stops.** Arrival sets the prompt, the
mode and (for ①–③) the dial, and clears the output. Nothing runs on its own and
nothing streams on navigation. Phase ④ deliberately inherits whatever the dial is
at, so the presenter can crank to 1.4 in base and step forward to hear the same
1.4 answered in format.

**Controls arriving still fade in** over 250ms. A fade is the opposite of a jump;
the instruction was that navigation must not *start* anything, and a reveal
doesn't.

### What is lost: the gates

The stage machine enforced discipline — the dial would not appear unless the
question had actually been run in base, and the offer would not appear unless the
dial had actually been moved. The footer hands that discipline to the presenter.
`stage.ts` and its twelve tests are deleted, and `phases.ts` is a plain ordered
list with a `reached` comparison. Recorded here so it reads as a decision rather
than an accident.

## 4 · The chrome

```
davinci-002  [ base ][ post-trained ]      temp ──●── 0.7 steady        ↺
             └─ fixed-width slot ─┘        └─ reserved from the start ─┘
```

**`davinci-002` never moves and never changes.** It is the machine's name, and
the machine does not change; only its training does.

**The switch is present from the first second with one cell.** A one-position
switch reads as a nameplate. `post-trained` fades into the slot beside it at
phase 4. There is no morph to serialise, which dissolves the two-phase
`AnimatePresence mode="wait"` crossfade flagged after the last build. The slot is
sized for both cells from the start, so nothing to its right ever shifts.

The dial's slot is reserved the same way — a fixed-width gap in the instrument
panel until phase 3, then the slider fades into it.

### The dial stays live in post-trained

The old design retracted the dial on the flip, arguing that post-training
flattened the dice. That argument was made by absence, and it was also close to
false — a post-trained model still has a temperature.

**The data gains per-band instruct completions**, so `instructAnswer: string`
becomes `instructAnswers: Record<Band, string>`, symmetrical with `continuations`.
The dial is then simply always live once revealed: no dimming, no disabled state,
no `—` readout, no rule to remember.

This buys a better beat than the one it replaces. Crank to 1.4 in base and the
machine asks *how do I reverse time? who is asking?*. Flip to post-trained at the
same 1.4, touch nothing, and it still answers the question — chattier, looser,
with an unsolicited aside, but in the shape you asked for. **The dice are still
there; the format doesn't care.** That is the true claim about what post-training
did, and it is the one the seniors in the room will recognise.

New copy required: two low-band and two high-band instruct completions (the
existing two become the mid band), plus `INSTRUCT_QUESTION_HIGH` and
`INSTRUCT_CONTINUE_HIGH` verdict lines. `verdictFor` already keys on band, so
this is new constants, not new machinery.

## 5 · Prompt tabs

```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ a half-written function │ a question   │
├─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┐
│ function reverseList(items) {                        │
│   return items.slice().reverse();                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The active tab shares the output panel's fill and opens its bottom edge into it,
so the tab strip and the generation window read as one object. Inactive tabs sit
muted above the panel's top border.

**The `PROMPT` eyebrow is deleted.** A tab strip does not need to announce that it
is a tab strip — and that removes one of the 11px labels.

In presenter mode phase 1 has a single tab; the second grows in rightward, so the
growth is horizontal and nothing below moves.

**These are plain buttons with `aria-pressed`, not `role="tab"`.** `role="tab"` is
in `ARROW_CONSUMING_SELECTOR`, so adopting it would silently swallow `→` on a
focused tab with nothing implementing roving focus — a live regression traded for
correct-looking ARIA. They become real tabs during the in-demo keyboard pass,
which is queued behind global shortcuts.

## 6 · The console speaks one line

A single fixed-height slot below the output panel, always rendered, showing at
most one line of secondary text:

1. the run's verdict, if a run has finished; otherwise
2. `temperature — how much the dice get to decide`, if the dial is visible and
   nothing has been run; otherwise
3. nothing.

This folds away two separate regions that each used to appear and disappear: the
bordered whisper row and the `↩ what just happened` affordance. Rule 2 also means
the whisper now labels the dial for cold readers in default mode, where it
previously had no home.

**The verdict fades in ~1.5s after streaming finishes.** The page still doesn't
beat the presenter to the line — it arrives after he's said it, quietly, agreeing
rather than announcing. Cold readers get the narration for free.

The `2022 · humans taught it a format` offer strip is **deleted**. Its date lives
in phase ④'s label and its sentence already lives in the `INSTRUCT_QUESTION`
verdict.

## 7 · Nothing moves

Five measures, in order of cost:

1. **The output panel gets a fixed height, not `min-h-40`.** Sized to the tallest
   prefix + completion across every prompt × band × mode, expressed as an
   `OUTPUT_LINES` constant with a test asserting no combination exceeds it — so
   adding copy later fails loudly instead of quietly reintroducing the jump.
   Overflow scrolls. **This means a visibly empty console at phase 1**, which is
   the accepted price of the `Run` button never moving.
2. **Fixed chrome row height**, with reserved slots for the switch's second cell
   and the dial.
3. **The always-present one-line slot** (§6).
4. **The offer strip and whisper row deleted** rather than animated.
5. **The footer is a fixed-height row**, present for the whole session in
   presenter mode.

## 8 · Session snapshot

"Stepping away and back should keep the state wherever it's at" is taken
literally. The module-level store grows from a single `Stage` to the full
snapshot:

```
phase, reached, mode, promptId, temp, output, verdict, lastRun
```

Step to Era II and back and the screen is identical — mid-demo, output and all.
A run in flight is stored as its *finished* text rather than frozen mid-stream,
so navigating away during streaming returns you to a completed run rather than a
truncated one.

A page reload still starts fresh. `↺` still re-arms deliberately: in presenter
mode it returns to phase ①; in default mode it clears the output and restores the
function prompt, base mode and 0.7.

## 9 · Code shape

**New, pure, TDD:**

- `phases.ts` — the ordered phase list, labels, arrival configuration, adjacency,
  `reached` comparison.
- `disposition.ts` — `dispositionFor({ presenter, phase, reached })`.

**New components:**

- `prompt-tabs.tsx` — the tab strip joined to the output panel.
- `phase-footer.tsx` — the accordion TOC and its arrows.

**Deleted:** `stage.ts`, `stage.test.ts`.

**Rewritten:** `index.tsx` (orchestration only), `console-chrome.tsx`,
`session-store.ts`.

**Amended:** `completions.ts` (`instructAnswers` per band), `selector.ts`
(`selectCompletion` reads the band in instruct mode too), `verdicts.ts` (two new
high-band lines), `step-keys.ts` + test (`isPresenterToggle`, `isTextEntryTarget`),
`masterclass.tsx` (read the flag, bind the chord, pass the prop).

**Untouched:** `selector.test.ts` beyond the instruct-band assertions it gains.

## Out of scope

- **Keyboard navigation inside the demo.** Phase arrows and prompt tabs are
  mouse-only. Global shortcuts are the prerequisite and are being solved first;
  `Shift+P` is admitted now only because it provably cannot collide with the one
  global binding that exists.
- **`aria-pressed` on the mode switch** and an accessible name for the slider —
  both pre-existing, both house-wide rather than regressions from this work.
- **Presenter mode for Era II–IV.** The flag is page-level so those demos can opt
  in later; none does in this pass.

```
┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ a half-written function │ a question   │
├─────────────────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┐
│ function reverseList(items) {                        │
│   return items.slice().reverse();                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The active tab shares the output panel's fill and opens its bottom edge into it,
so the tab strip and the generation window read as one object. Inactive tabs sit
muted above the panel's top border.

**The `PROMPT` eyebrow is deleted.** A tab strip does not need to announce that it
is a tab strip — and that removes one of the 11px labels.

In presenter mode phase 1 has a single tab; the second grows in rightward, so the
growth is horizontal and nothing below moves.

**These are plain buttons with `aria-pressed`, not `role="tab"`.** `role="tab"` is
in `ARROW_CONSUMING_SELECTOR`, so adopting it would silently swallow `→` on a
focused tab with nothing implementing roving focus — a live regression traded for
correct-looking ARIA. They become real tabs during the in-demo keyboard pass,
which is queued behind global shortcuts.

## 6 · The console speaks one line

A single fixed-height slot below the output panel, always rendered, showing at
most one line of secondary text:

1. the run's verdict, if a run has finished; otherwise
2. `temperature — how much the dice get to decide`, if the dial is visible and
   nothing has been run; otherwise
3. nothing.

This folds away two separate regions that each used to appear and disappear: the
bordered whisper row and the `↩ what just happened` affordance. Rule 2 also means
the whisper now labels the dial for cold readers in default mode, where it
previously had no home.

**The verdict fades in ~1.5s after streaming finishes.** The page still doesn't
beat the presenter to the line — it arrives after he's said it, quietly, agreeing
rather than announcing. Cold readers get the narration for free.

The `2022 · humans taught it a format` offer strip is **deleted**. Its date lives
in phase ④'s label and its sentence already lives in the `INSTRUCT_QUESTION`
verdict.

## 7 · Nothing moves

Five measures, in order of cost:

1. **The output panel gets a fixed height, not `min-h-40`.** Sized to the tallest
   prefix + completion across every prompt × band × mode, expressed as an
   `OUTPUT_LINES` constant with a test asserting no combination exceeds it — so
   adding copy later fails loudly instead of quietly reintroducing the jump.
   Overflow scrolls. **This means a visibly empty console at phase 1**, which is
   the accepted price of the `Run` button never moving.
2. **Fixed chrome row height**, with reserved slots for the switch's second cell
   and the dial.
3. **The always-present one-line slot** (§6).
4. **The offer strip and whisper row deleted** rather than animated.
5. **The footer is a fixed-height row**, present for the whole session in
   presenter mode.

## 8 · Session snapshot

"Stepping away and back should keep the state wherever it's at" is taken
literally. The module-level store grows from a single `Stage` to the full
snapshot:

```
phase, reached, mode, promptId, temp, output, verdict, lastRun
```

Step to Era II and back and the screen is identical — mid-demo, output and all.
A run in flight is stored as its *finished* text rather than frozen mid-stream,
so navigating away during streaming returns you to a completed run rather than a
truncated one.

A page reload still starts fresh. `↺` still re-arms deliberately: in presenter
mode it returns to phase ①; in default mode it clears the output and restores the
function prompt, base mode and 0.7.

## 9 · Code shape

**New, pure, TDD:**

- `phases.ts` — the ordered phase list, labels, arrival configuration, adjacency,
  `reached` comparison.
- `disposition.ts` — `dispositionFor({ presenter, phase, reached })`.

**New components:**

- `prompt-tabs.tsx` — the tab strip joined to the output panel.
- `phase-footer.tsx` — the accordion TOC and its arrows.

**Deleted:** `stage.ts`, `stage.test.ts`.

**Rewritten:** `index.tsx` (orchestration only), `console-chrome.tsx`,
`session-store.ts`.

**Amended:** `completions.ts` (`instructAnswers` per band), `selector.ts`
(`selectCompletion` reads the band in instruct mode too), `verdicts.ts` (two new
high-band lines), `step-keys.ts` + test (`isPresenterToggle`, `isTextEntryTarget`),
`masterclass.tsx` (read the flag, bind the chord, pass the prop).

**Untouched:** `selector.test.ts` beyond the instruct-band assertions it gains.

## Out of scope

- **Keyboard navigation inside the demo.** Phase arrows and prompt tabs are
  mouse-only. Global shortcuts are the prerequisite and are being solved first;
  `Shift+P` is admitted now only because it provably cannot collide with the one
  global binding that exists.
- **`aria-pressed` on the mode switch** and an accessible name for the slider —
  both pre-existing, both house-wide rather than regressions from this work.
- **Presenter mode for Era II–IV.** The flag is page-level so those demos can opt
  in later; none does in this pass.

content.text:
Spec written and committed as `3965b6a` → `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-25-masterclass-era1-presenter-transport-design.md`.

Four things I settled during self-review that weren't explicit in our conversation — worth your eye before I write the plan:

- **`↺` now resets `reached`, not just the phase.** Re-arming has to close the gates again, otherwise you can't rehearse the reveal a second time. Reload still starts fresh either way.
- **Toggling `Shift+P` mid-session preserves the snapshot.** Leaving presenter mode keeps your phase in the store and just shows everything; coming back restores the same highlight. The chord changes what's displayed, never what's happened.
- **Disclosure follows `reached`, the footer highlight follows `phase`.** Jumping back to ① after reaching ④ doesn't take the dial away. Closing gates would make the footer a trap — step back to check something, lose the control you were about to use.
- **Phase ④ inherits the dial; ①–③ reset it to 0.7.** That's what preserves the beat you bought with the live dial: crank to 1.4 in base, step forward, same 1.4, and it answers anyway.

One thing I want to flag rather than bury: the spec deletes `stage.ts` and its twelve tests. Those tests encode the gates — *the dial won't open unless you actually ran the question in base; the offer won't open unless you actually moved the dial*. You said delete the gates and I agree with the reasoning, but that's real verification going away, and `phases.ts` replaces it with something much simpler (an ordered list and a `reached` comparison). Net test count will likely go **down** before the new pure modules bring it back up. Not a problem, just not the usual direction.

Please review the spec and tell me if you want changes before I write the implementation plan.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.2.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review
