# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

Related: [[project_ts7_migration]]

Supporting files: `session-store.ts` (module-level snapshot persisted across mount/unmount so stepping the presenter deck back doesn't lose state), `verdicts.ts` (pure `verdictFor()` lookup — always returns a string, no throw path), `selector.ts`/`completions.ts` (completion text lookup).

### 1. Sequencing logic location
All of it lives in `index.tsx`: a local `streaming` boolean, a `timer` ref holding the `setInterval` id, a `target` ref holding the full completion string, and a `useEffect` that watches `{streaming, lastRun, verdict}` to schedule the verdict.

### 2. What ends the stream
Not a fixed total-duration timer and not computed from text length up front — it's **per-character**, driven by a `setInterval` ticking every `STREAM_MS = 18`ms:

```js
const STREAM_MS = 18;
...
let i = 0;
timer.current = setInterval(() => {
  i += 1;
  setSnap((s) => ({ ...s, output: full.slice(0, i) }));
  if (i >= full.length) {
    stopTimer();          // clears interval, setStreaming(false)
  }
}, STREAM_MS);
```
So total stream time scales with `full.length * 18ms`; completion is detected inside the interval callback itself once `i >= full.length`.

### 3. Verdict delay
Exactly **1500ms**, via a named constant, fired from a separate effect keyed off `streaming` flipping to false:

```js
const VERDICT_DELAY_MS = 1500;
...
useEffect(() => {
  const id =
    !streaming && lastRun !== null && verdict === null
      ? setTimeout(() => patch({ verdict: verdictFor(lastRun) }), VERDICT_DELAY_MS)
      : null;
  return () => { if (id) clearTimeout(id); };
}, [lastRun, patch, streaming, verdict]);
```

### 4. Known bugs / edge cases
- No stuck-forever case found in the current version — `git log` shows a prior real bug (`a257f69`, "stream-safe Era I toggle") where clicking a prompt/mode button mid-stream left a stale interval running; it's already fixed by calling `stopTimer()` in every handler (`handleModeChange`, `handlePromptClick`, `goToPhase`, `handleReset`) before mutating state.
- `prefers-reduced-motion` takes a separate branch that sets `output: full` immediately and never sets `streaming: true`; it correctly still routes through the same verdict effect, so no gap there.
- Minor fragility: `selectCompletion(runPromptId, ...)` in `selector.ts` silently returns `""` if `runPromptId` doesn't match any `PROMPTS` entry, while `run()`'s own `runPrompt` lookup falls back to `PROMPTS[0]`. If `promptId` ever desyncs from the `PROMPTS` list (e.g., stale session-store data after a content edit), you'd get an empty completion streamed against a `lastRun` describing a different prompt — verdict still appears (band/mode/isQuestion are independent of the text), just describing text that wasn't actually shown. content.text:
## Review: Era I presenter transport (`b329db4..03511be`, 6 commits)

Verified: `bun test` **106 pass / 0 fail**, `bun run typecheck` clean, working tree == HEAD. Findings 1–3 were reproduced live in a browser against the running dev server on :3001, not inferred.

### Strengths (specific, and they matter for the three findings below)

- The SSR-safety claim in `session-store.ts:38-42` is **actually true**. `useState(getSnapshot)` (`index.tsx:43`) only *reads* the module-level store; every write goes through an effect. No cross-request leak, no hydration mismatch. I checked for this specifically.
- The mid-stream unmount save (`index.tsx:64-73`) is correct. `latest.current` can lag by at most one interval tick, and the only field that changes during streaming (`output`) is the one the cleanup overrides with `target.current`. Cleanup ordering (defined second, after the no-cleanup `[snap]` effect) puts the last write where it belongs.
- The verdict timeout (`index.tsx:114-129`) returns a cleanup on every path, and the click→cleanup→reschedule sequence is synchronous within React's commit, so a pending timeout cannot interleave with a control change. No stale-closure hazard: `patch` is functional.
- No throw paths found. `phaseFor`, the `PROMPTS.find` sites, `adjacentPhase` and `selectCompletion` all have total fallbacks; a `full` of `""` still terminates the interval on the first tick.
- Deleting `stage.ts` is the right call, and `dispositionFor` is genuinely the only reconciliation point — which is precisely how I found finding 1.

---

### Critical

**1. `Shift+P` after touching any control in default mode drops presenter mode into a state the four beats cannot produce — and it leaks the demo's punchline on beat ①.**
`index.tsx:193-196` · `disposition.ts:31-36`

`dispositionFor` takes only `{furthest, presenter}`. It never sees `mode`, `promptId` or `temp`. Nothing else reconciles them. So the toggle can hide a control that is currently *in use*.

Reproduced live at 1440px:
1. Default view. Click `a question`. Click `post-trained`. (Exactly what the Task-7 walk's Step 3 does.)
2. Press `Shift+P`.

Observed DOM:
```
footer:      ① autocomplete   (furthest = "autocomplete")
mode cells:  [ base ]              aria-pressed="false"   ← nothing lit; snap.mode is "instruct"
tabs:        [ a half-written function ]  aria-pressed="false"  ← nothing lit
panel shows: "// how do I reverse a list in JavaScript?"   ← the *other* prompt
dial:        absent, temp still live
```
Then I pressed `Run` at beat ①:
```
output: "Copy the array first, then reverse it: const reversed = items.slice().reverse()…"
status: "Now it answers. Not because it became something else — because humans
         taught it the format. That flip is the ChatGPT moment."
```
On the projector, at the "it's just autocomplete" beat, the console shows an unlit `base` nameplate over a question prompt, answers like a post-trained model, and prints the ChatGPT-moment line — the payoff of the entire era — as beat one's verdict.

Recovery is one click (`base`, the visible tab, or `↺`), but only if he notices; the console gives no signal it is lying. The same happens on a soft navigation back to `?presenter=true` while the module store holds a default-mode session.

Why this got through: the plan's Task 7 Step 4 says *"Press `Shift+P`. Then press `↺` to close the gates"* — the `↺` masks the bug, and `↺` is the only thing that resyncs `furthest` with the machine. Spec §8 meanwhile advertises the toggle as safe: *"The toggle changes what is displayed, never what has happened."* It changes what has happened without changing what is displayed to match.

Smallest fixes, both inside the existing seam: either feed `mode`/`promptId`/`temp` into `dispositionFor` and OR the gates open (`showPostTrainedCell: reached(furthest,"taught") || mode === "instruct"`, etc.), or bump `furthest` in `handleModeChange` / `handlePromptClick` / `handleTempChange` so the snapshot can never outrun its own disclosure. The first keeps `dispositionFor` the single reconciliation point, which is the design's stated intent.

---

### Important

**2. `?presenter=1` — the entry URL the spec documents — does not enable presenter mode.**
`masterclass.tsx:42-45`

nuqs `parseAsBoolean` is `parse: (v) => v.toLowerCase() === "true"` (`node_modules/nuqs/dist/index.js:168-171`). Anything that isn't the literal `true` falls to the default `false`. Spec §1 says in bold: *"**Entry is `?presenter=1`**."*

Confirmed live: navigating to `?step=completion&presenter=1` renders no footer, both mode cells, both tabs and the dial — the default view. Only `?presenter=true` works.

Failure scenario: Eric bookmarks the URL the spec told him to, opens it on the borrowed laptop, and gets the fully-populated shared-link view with no footer. It degrades rather than breaking (mild, per the spec's own philosophy), but the documented entry point is dead. Fix is one line either way — accept `1`/`""` with a custom parser, or correct the spec to `?presenter=true`.

**3. Below the `sm` breakpoint the chrome row is clipped, and the dial and `↺` become unreachable.**
`console-chrome.tsx:54`

The row went from `flex flex-wrap … gap-y-3 py-2.5` (wrapping, auto height) to `flex h-14 items-center` with every child `shrink-0`, no wrap and no `overflow-x`, inside a parent that is `overflow-hidden` (`index.tsx:207`).

Measured live:

| viewport | clipped px | reset button |
|---|---|---|
| 1440 / 1280 / 768 | 0 | visible |
| 640 | 0 | visible (5px margin) |
| 500 | 127 | **127px past the right edge** |
| 390 | 237 | **227px past the right edge; slider also fully outside** |

Screenshot at 390px shows the row reading `davinci-002 [base][post-trained] TEMP` and cut mid-word. The temperature dial, its `0.7 · mid` readout and the `↺` reset are gone, with no scroll to reach them.

This is a regression from this diff, and it lands squarely on the audience the default mode exists for — spec §1: *"this is what a visitor gets from a shared link, and it is a complete demo."* On a phone it is not a complete demo. A `sm:h-14` + `flex-wrap` fallback, or `overflow-x-auto` on the row, restores it without touching the ≥640px geometry the fixed-height work was for.

---

### Minor

**4. The status row's fixed `h-14` overflows its own borders on narrow viewports.** `index.tsx:244-248`. Measured: the longest verdict (`INSTRUCT_QUESTION_HIGH`) renders 80px tall at 390px and 60px at 640px, inside a 56px row with `items-center` and `overflow: visible`. The text spills 12px above and below, across the border into the Run row. Fine at ≥768px (40px).

**5. The `OUTPUT_COLUMNS = 72` guard only holds above ~760px viewport.** `completions.ts:23-24`, asserted in `completions.test.ts:66-72`, consumed as a fixed height at `index.tsx:225-228`. Measured: the widest line renders at 630px; the `pre`'s inner width is 908px at 1280 and 652px at 768, but 524px at 640 and 322px at 390. Below ~760px lines wrap, the 9-line reservation is exceeded, and the panel scrolls without following the stream — so the cursor runs off the bottom. The spec accepts "overflow scrolls"; the gap is that a test named "no line is wide enough to wrap into a second one" asserts something the layout only honours at one end of the range, and nothing records that.

**6. `NUMERALS` and `PHASES` are not coupled.** `phase-footer.tsx:7,66`. A fifth phase makes `NUMERALS[index]` `undefined` — a silently blank cell, no throw. One assertion in `phases.test.ts` would close it.

**7. Streaming can split a surrogate pair.** `index.tsx:102` — `full.slice(0, i)` slices by code unit, and the high-band `reverse-fn` continuation contains `🦆` (`completions.ts:31`). One 18ms frame of a replacement glyph, reachable in default mode at temp ≥ 1.0. Cosmetic.

---

### Triage of the ledger's three deferred minors

**`isArrowConsumingTarget` missing the `typeof Element !== "undefined"` guard** (`step-keys.ts:52-57`) — **can wait.** Not reachable. Its only production caller is the keydown handler inside `useEffect` (`masterclass.tsx:47-55`), which is client-only, where `Element` always exists. The guard on `isTextEntryTarget` exists because `step-keys.test.ts` calls it directly with `null` under Bun; there is no equivalent direct test for the arrow predicate. Worth adding for symmetry after the talk, not before.

**Missing `focus-visible` ring in `prompt-tabs.tsx:36` and `phase-footer.tsx:20,52`** — **can wait.** I checked what `stepper-header.tsx:25` actually adds: `focus-visible:outline-hidden` *plus* a custom bg/text treatment. The new components omit `outline-hidden`, so they keep the browser's default focus ring (Preflight doesn't remove it; the only global rule is `outline-ring/50` at `packages/design-system/globals.css:148`, which sets colour, not style). Keyboard focus is therefore still visible — this is house-style inconsistency, not an accessibility break. Consistent with the spec's out-of-scope note on in-demo keyboard work.

**Collapsed footer numerals with no accessible name beyond the glyph** (`phase-footer.tsx:66`) — **can wait.** Presenter-mode-only, mouse-only by explicit design, and the active cell already carries `aria-current="step"`. Cheap to fix (`aria-label={phase.label}` on the button) whenever the in-demo keyboard pass lands.

## Review: Era I presenter transport (`b329db4..03511be`, 6 commits)

Verified: `bun test` **106 pass / 0 fail**, `bun run typecheck` clean, working tree == HEAD. Findings 1–3 were reproduced live in a browser against the running dev server on :3001, not inferred.

### Strengths (specific, and they matter for the three findings below)

- The SSR-safety claim in `session-store.ts:38-42` is **actually true**. `useState(getSnapshot)` (`index.tsx:43`) only *reads* the module-level store; every write goes through an effect. No cross-request leak, no hydration mismatch. I checked for this specifically.
- The mid-stream unmount save (`index.tsx:64-73`) is correct. `latest.current` can lag by at most one interval tick, and the only field that changes during streaming (`output`) is the one the cleanup overrides with `target.current`. Cleanup ordering (defined second, after the no-cleanup `[snap]` effect) puts the last write where it belongs.
- The verdict timeout (`index.tsx:114-129`) returns a cleanup on every path, and the click→cleanup→reschedule sequence is synchronous within React's commit, so a pending timeout cannot interleave with a control change. No stale-closure hazard: `patch` is functional.
- No throw paths found. `phaseFor`, the `PROMPTS.find` sites, `adjacentPhase` and `selectCompletion` all have total fallbacks; a `full` of `""` still terminates the interval on the first tick.
- Deleting `stage.ts` is the right call, and `dispositionFor` is genuinely the only reconciliation point — which is precisely how I found finding 1.

---

### Critical

**1. `Shift+P` after touching any control in default mode drops presenter mode into a state the four beats cannot produce — and it leaks the demo's punchline on beat ①.**
`index.tsx:193-196` · `disposition.ts:31-36`

`dispositionFor` takes only `{furthest, presenter}`. It never sees `mode`, `promptId` or `temp`. Nothing else reconciles them. So the toggle can hide a control that is currently *in use*.

Reproduced live at 1440px:
1. Default view. Click `a question`. Click `post-trained`. (Exactly what the Task-7 walk's Step 3 does.)
2. Press `Shift+P`.

Observed DOM:
```
footer:      ① autocomplete   (furthest = "autocomplete")
mode cells:  [ base ]              aria-pressed="false"   ← nothing lit; snap.mode is "instruct"
tabs:        [ a half-written function ]  aria-pressed="false"  ← nothing lit
panel shows: "// how do I reverse a list in JavaScript?"   ← the *other* prompt
dial:        absent, temp still live
```
Then I pressed `Run` at beat ①:
```
output: "Copy the array first, then reverse it: const reversed = items.slice().reverse()…"
status: "Now it answers. Not because it became something else — because humans
         taught it the format. That flip is the ChatGPT moment."
```
On the projector, at the "it's just autocomplete" beat, the console shows an unlit `base` nameplate over a question prompt, answers like a post-trained model, and prints the ChatGPT-moment line — the payoff of the entire era — as beat one's verdict.

Recovery is one click (`base`, the visible tab, or `↺`), but only if he notices; the console gives no signal it is lying. The same happens on a soft navigation back to `?presenter=true` while the module store holds a default-mode session.

Why this got through: the plan's Task 7 Step 4 says *"Press `Shift+P`. Then press `↺` to close the gates"* — the `↺` masks the bug, and `↺` is the only thing that resyncs `furthest` with the machine. Spec §8 meanwhile advertises the toggle as safe: *"The toggle changes what is displayed, never what has happened."* It changes what has happened without changing what is displayed to match.

Smallest fixes, both inside the existing seam: either feed `mode`/`promptId`/`temp` into `dispositionFor` and OR the gates open (`showPostTrainedCell: reached(furthest,"taught") || mode === "instruct"`, etc.), or bump `furthest` in `handleModeChange` / `handlePromptClick` / `handleTempChange` so the snapshot can never outrun its own disclosure. The first keeps `dispositionFor` the single reconciliation point, which is the design's stated intent.

---

### Important

**2. `?presenter=1` — the entry URL the spec documents — does not enable presenter mode.**
`masterclass.tsx:42-45`

nuqs `parseAsBoolean` is `parse: (v) => v.toLowerCase() === "true"` (`node_modules/nuqs/dist/index.js:168-171`). Anything that isn't the literal `true` falls to the default `false`. Spec §1 says in bold: *"**Entry is `?presenter=1`**."*

Confirmed live: navigating to `?step=completion&presenter=1` renders no footer, both mode cells, both tabs and the dial — the default view. Only `?presenter=true` works.

Failure scenario: Eric bookmarks the URL the spec told him to, opens it on the borrowed laptop, and gets the fully-populated shared-link view with no footer. It degrades rather than breaking (mild, per the spec's own philosophy), but the documented entry point is dead. Fix is one line either way — accept `1`/`""` with a custom parser, or correct the spec to `?presenter=true`.

**3. Below the `sm` breakpoint the chrome row is clipped, and the dial and `↺` become unreachable.**
`console-chrome.tsx:54`

The row went from `flex flex-wrap … gap-y-3 py-2.5` (wrapping, auto height) to `flex h-14 items-center` with every child `shrink-0`, no wrap and no `overflow-x`, inside a parent that is `overflow-hidden` (`index.tsx:207`).

Measured live:

| viewport | clipped px | reset button |
|---|---|---|
| 1440 / 1280 / 768 | 0 | visible |
| 640 | 0 | visible (5px margin) |
| 500 | 127 | **127px past the right edge** |
| 390 | 237 | **227px past the right edge; slider also fully outside** |

Screenshot at 390px shows the row reading `davinci-002 [base][post-trained] TEMP` and cut mid-word. The temperature dial, its `0.7 · mid` readout and the `↺` reset are gone, with no scroll to reach them.

This is a regression from this diff, and it lands squarely on the audience the default mode exists for — spec §1: *"this is what a visitor gets from a shared link, and it is a complete demo."* On a phone it is not a complete demo. A `sm:h-14` + `flex-wrap` fallback, or `overflow-x-auto` on the row, restores it without touching the ≥640px geometry the fixed-height work was for.

---

### Minor

**4. The status row's fixed `h-14` overflows its own borders on narrow viewports.** `index.tsx:244-248`. Measured: the longest verdict (`INSTRUCT_QUESTION_HIGH`) renders 80px tall at 390px and 60px at 640px, inside a 56px row with `items-center` and `overflow: visible`. The text spills 12px above and below, across the border into the Run row. Fine at ≥768px (40px).

**5. The `OUTPUT_COLUMNS = 72` guard only holds above ~760px viewport.** `completions.ts:23-24`, asserted in `completions.test.ts:66-72`, consumed as a fixed height at `index.tsx:225-228`. Measured: the widest line renders at 630px; the `pre`'s inner width is 908px at 1280 and 652px at 768, but 524px at 640 and 322px at 390. Below ~760px lines wrap, the 9-line reservation is exceeded, and the panel scrolls without following the stream — so the cursor runs off the bottom. The spec accepts "overflow scrolls"; the gap is that a test named "no line is wide enough to wrap into a second one" asserts something the layout only honours at one end of the range, and nothing records that.

**6. `NUMERALS` and `PHASES` are not coupled.** `phase-footer.tsx:7,66`. A fifth phase makes `NUMERALS[index]` `undefined` — a silently blank cell, no throw. One assertion in `phases.test.ts` would close it.

**7. Streaming can split a surrogate pair.** `index.tsx:102` — `full.slice(0, i)` slices by code unit, and the high-band `reverse-fn` continuation contains `🦆` (`completions.ts:31`). One 18ms frame of a replacement glyph, reachable in default mode at temp ≥ 1.0. Cosmetic.

---

### Triage of the ledger's three deferred minors

**`isArrowConsumingTarget` missing the `typeof Element !== "undefined"` guard** (`step-keys.ts:52-57`) — **can wait.** Not reachable. Its only production caller is the keydown handler inside `useEffect` (`masterclass.tsx:47-55`), which is client-only, where `Element` always exists. The guard on `isTextEntryTarget` exists because `step-keys.test.ts` calls it directly with `null` under Bun; there is no equivalent direct test for the arrow predicate. Worth adding for symmetry after the talk, not before.

**Missing `focus-visible` ring in `prompt-tabs.tsx:36` and `phase-footer.tsx:20,52`** — **can wait.** I checked what `stepper-header.tsx:25` actually adds: `focus-visible:outline-hidden` *plus* a custom bg/text treatment. The new components omit `outline-hidden`, so they keep the browser's default focus ring (Preflight doesn't remove it; the only global rule is `outline-ring/50` at `packages/design-system/globals.css:148`, which sets colour, not style). Keyboard focus is therefore still visible — this is house-style inconsistency, not an accessibility break. Consistent with the spec's out-of-scope note on in-demo keyboard work.

**Collapsed footer numerals with no accessible name beyond the glyph** (`phase-footer.tsx:66`) — **can wait.** Presenter-mode-only, mouse-only by explicit design, and the active cell already carries `aria-current="step"`. Cheap to fix (`aria-label={phase.label}` on the button) whenever the in-demo keyboard pass lands.

---

### Assessment

**Ready to ship: with fixes.** Finding 1 before the 28th — it is a projector-visible failure that spoils the era's punchline on its first beat, and its trigger (touch a control, press the chord the spec advertises as safe) is one the presenter is invited to perform. Finding 2 is a one-liner and the spec is currently wrong about how to start the thing. Finding 3 can slip until after the talk if the shared link's phone audience can wait a day, but it undoes the redesign's own justification for default mode.

Everything the spec set out to prove — the Run button not moving, the state machine surviving navigation mid-stream, the dial being live on both sides, nothing running on arrival — is correctly built and independently verified. The defect is not in the machinery; it is that `dispositionFor` inherited only half of what `stage.ts` used to reconcile.

I've identified three real issues from the review: a critical design flaw where `dispositionFor` isn't accounting for mode and promptId, a spec mismatch on how the presenter parameter should be formatted, and a mobile regression. I'll dispatch one fix with all three findings listed, then do a focused re-review of just those changes.

Looking at the remaining findings, 4 and 5 are viewport-related issues that tie into the mobile regression, so I'll bundle those together. Findings 6 and 7 are small fixes, but 7 involves tweaking the streaming loop to handle surrogate pairs correctly — that's the kind of change I'd rather defer right before a talk. I'll include 6 but leave 7 as a documented minor for later.

For the first finding, I'm going with the approach of passing mode and promptId directly into `dispositionFor` and opening up the gates with an OR condition — that keeps the disposition logic as the single source of truth for reconciliation.

Actually, the dial case exposes a problem with that approach: if someone switches to presenter mode after adjusting temperature in default mode, the dial disappears but the temperature stays at 1.4, which is misleading. The cleaner fix is to bump `furthest` whenever a control gets used in default mode, so the snapshot tracks what's actually been touched. That way toggling modes can never hide something in active use, and it handles temperature and other controls uniformly.

The tradeoff is that each handler (mode change, prompt click, temperature adjustment) would need to independently bump `furthest`, spreading the logic around. A better approach: extract a pure function that infers the minimum phase required by the current machine configuration—checking whether instruct mode is active, temperature differs from the default, or a specific prompt has been selected—then compute `furthest` as the maximum of the stored value and this inferred phase at the single point where disposition gets calculated.

Applying this at render time rather than mutating state keeps things cleaner and avoids extra effect logic. The footer would still display beat ① while the machine is post-trained, which is actually fine—the presenter sees the correct controls lit up and can interact with any beat without confusion. Updating the phase derivation... At beat ② in presenter mode, the dial isn't visible so dragging the temperature slider would be unreachable anyway. At beat ① there's only one tab and one switch—nothing to interact with that would trigger a later phase. So the derivation logic is effectively inert within presenter mode and only activates during the default-to-presenter transition, which is exactly what we need. This approach is clean and testable without spreading logic elsewhere. Now I'm working on a custom parser to handle both cases. I'm debating whether to use media queries or a simpler approach for the responsive height. The cleanest pragmatic solution is to keep the fixed height everywhere and let the content wrap and scroll below the breakpoint, which aligns with the spec's overflow behavior anyway.

The real issue is documenting that the guard's width dependency needs a note in the code and test name. I'll add assertions in the test file for the numerals length, then dispatch a fix with all these changes against the current HEAD.

Add a pure function to `demos/era1-playground/phases.ts` that maps a machine configuration back to the earliest phase that could have produced it:

```ts
export function phaseImpliedBy({
  mode,
  promptId,
  temp,
}: {
  mode: Mode;
  promptId: string;
  temp: number;
}): PhaseId
```

Rules, checked in this order (later beats win):
- `mode === "instruct"` → `"taught"`
- `temp !== INITIAL_TEMP` → `"dial"`
- `promptId` is the question prompt's id → `"unanswered"`
- otherwise → `"autocomplete"`

Derive the question prompt's id from `PROMPTS` (`PROMPTS.find((p) => p.isQuestion)`), not a hardcoded string. `INITIAL_TEMP` is exported from `./selector`.

Then in `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx`, at the point where the disposition is derived, fold the implied phase into **both** the furthest phase and the current phase, at render time — no new state, no new effects:

```tsx
const implied = phaseImpliedBy({
  mode: snap.mode,
  promptId: snap.promptId,
  temp: snap.temp,
});
const furthest = furthestOf(snap.furthest, implied);
const phase = furthestOf(snap.phase, implied);
```

Use `furthest` for `dispositionFor` and `phase` for `<PhaseFooter current=...>`. Both `furthestOf` calls are monotone, so this can only ever open gates and advance the highlight, never close or rewind them.

Why folding it into `phase` too, and not just `furthest`: without it the footer would highlight `① autocomplete` while the machine is demonstrably post-trained — the projector would show the wrong beat name over the right output. Within presenter mode this whole derivation is a no-op (at beat ① there is nothing on screen to touch that implies a later beat), and stepping backwards still works because `goToPhase` reconfigures the machine, so the implied phase follows the arrival config down.

`demos/era1-playground/console-chrome.tsx:54` is `flex h-14 items-center` with every child `shrink-0`, no wrapping, no horizontal overflow, inside a parent that is `overflow-hidden`. Measured: at 500px viewport 127px is clipped; at 390px, 237px — the temperature slider, its readout and the `↺` reset are all off-screen with no way to reach them.

Something in the shape of `flex min-h-14 flex-wrap items-center gap-y-2 py-2 sm:h-14 sm:flex-nowrap sm:py-0` — verify the exact classes give a pixel-identical row at ≥640px, because a fixed-height chrome above `sm` is the point of the redesign.

`index.tsx` renders the verdict slot as a fixed `h-14` with `items-center`. The longest verdict renders 80px tall at 390px and 60px at 640px, spilling across the border into the Run row. Same treatment as Finding 3: `min-h-14` plus vertical padding below `sm`, exact `h-14` at `sm` and up.

`demos/era1-playground/phase-footer.tsx` indexes a four-element `NUMERALS` array by phase index. A fifth phase would render a silently blank cell. ## Finding 1 — CRITICAL. Toggling into presenter mode can hide a control that is currently in use.

`dispositionFor({ furthest, presenter })` in `demos/era1-playground/disposition.ts` decides what is on screen from the furthest phase visited. It never sees `mode`, `promptId` or `temp`, and nothing else reconciles them. So:

```ts
export function phaseImpliedBy({
  mode,
  promptId,
  temp,
}: {
  mode: Mode;
  promptId: string;
  temp: number;
}): PhaseId
```

Rules, checked in this order (later beats win):
- `mode === "instruct"` → `"taught"`
- `temp !== INITIAL_TEMP` → `"dial"`
- `promptId` is the question prompt's id → `"unanswered"`
- otherwise → `"autocomplete"`

Then in `demos/era1-playground/index.tsx`, at the point where the disposition is derived, fold the implied phase into **both** the furthest phase and the current phase, at render time — no new state, no new effects:

```tsx
const implied = phaseImpliedBy({
  mode: snap.mode,
  promptId: snap.promptId,
  temp: snap.temp,
});
const furthest = furthestOf(snap.furthest, implied);
const phase = furthestOf(snap.phase, implied);
```

Use `furthest` for `dispositionFor` and `phase` for `<PhaseFooter current=...>`. Both `furthestOf` calls are monotone, so this can only ever open gates and advance the highlight, never close or rewind them.

`completions.test.ts` has a test named "no line is wide enough to wrap into a second one", and `OUTPUT_COLUMNS = 72` in `completions.ts`. Files live under `apps/web/app/[locale]/learn/masterclass-28-07-2026/` — **quote paths, they contain square brackets.**

**The six findings, with the fix each was required to implement:**

**1 (Critical).** `dispositionFor({furthest, presenter})` never saw `mode`/`promptId`/`temp`, so pressing `Shift+P` after using a control in default mode hid controls that were in use — and pressing `Run` at beat ① then printed the ChatGPT-moment verdict, the era's payoff, on the first beat. Required fix: a pure `phaseImpliedBy({mode, promptId, temp}): PhaseId` in `phases.ts` mapping a machine configuration back to the earliest phase that could have produced it (`instruct` → `taught`; `temp !== INITIAL_TEMP` → `dial`; question prompt → `unanswered`; else `autocomplete`, later beats winning), with the question prompt's id derived from `PROMPTS.find(p => p.isQuestion)` rather than hardcoded. Then in `index.tsx`, at render time with no new state or effects, fold the implied phase into **both** the furthest phase and the current phase via `furthestOf`, and use those for `dispositionFor` and `<PhaseFooter current=…>`.
  Check specifically: is the fold monotone (can only open gates and advance the highlight, never close or rewind)? Does stepping backwards through phases still work — `goToPhase` reconfigures the machine, so the implied phase must follow the arrival config back down rather than pinning the footer forward? Is the derivation genuinely a no-op while already inside presenter mode?

**2 (Important).** nuqs `parseAsBoolean` only accepts the literal string `true`, so `?presenter=1` — the entry URL the spec documents in bold — silently yielded the default view. Required fix: a `createParser` accepting `1`, `true` (any case) and the bare `?presenter` (empty string), serialising to `"1"`, keeping `.withDefault(false)` and keeping `.withOptions({ history: "replace" })`. **Replace-history is load-bearing** — push would put every toggle in the back stack, so the page's global ArrowLeft would start undoing presenter mode instead of stepping eras. Confirm it survived the edit.

**3 (Important).** The chrome row was `flex h-14 items-center` with `shrink-0` children, no wrap, no overflow, inside an `overflow-hidden` parent — clipping 127px at 500px viewport and 237px at 390px, losing the temperature dial and the `↺` reset entirely. Required fix: wrap and grow below the `sm` breakpoint while keeping **pixel-identical** fixed geometry at `sm` and up, since a fixed-height chrome above `sm` is the entire point of the redesign.

**4 (Minor).** The verdict slot's fixed `h-14` let the longest verdict spill 80px at 390px / 60px at 640px across its border into the Run row. Same treatment: `min-h` plus padding below `sm`, exact `h-14` at `sm` and up.

**5 (Minor).** Documentation only. The `OUTPUT_COLUMNS = 72` guard's premise holds only above ~760px viewport. Required: extend the doc comment in `completions.ts` to state the reservation holds at projector widths and narrower viewports scroll instead, and rename the misleading test. **Constants and layout were explicitly not to change** — verify they didn't.

**6 (Minor).** `NUMERALS` (4 elements) is indexed by phase index in `phase-footer.tsx` with no coupling to `PHASES`. Required: an assertion in `phases.test.ts` that `PHASES.length` is 4, named so the coupling is discoverable from either end.

**Explicitly out of scope — if the fix diff touched any of these, that is new breakage:** `isArrowConsumingTarget`'s missing `typeof Element` guard; the missing `focus-visible` ring on `prompt-tabs.tsx`/`phase-footer.tsx`; accessible names on collapsed footer numerals; the `🦆` surrogate-pair split in the streaming loop in `index.tsx`; and `role="tab"` on the prompt tabs (it is in `ARROW_CONSUMING_SELECTOR` and would break era navigation — `aria-pressed` is correct).

**Constraints the fix had to respect:** suite was 106 pass / 0 fail and had to end higher without breaking anything (report claims 113); named exports only; `interface` over `type`; alphabetically sorted object keys.

**You may verify in a browser** — a dev server is ALREADY RUNNING on port 3001; do NOT start one (Next 16 refuses a second for the same project directory). **Finding 1 (Critical) — ADDRESSED.** `phaseImpliedBy` is a pure function in `apps/web/app/[locale]/learn/masterclass-28-07-2026/demos/era1-playground/phases.ts:83-102`, with the question prompt derived at `phases.ts:74` (`PROMPTS.find((p) => p.isQuestion)?.id`, not hardcoded); precedence is instruct → dial → question → autocomplete, later beats winning. - Backwards stepping works: ← walked ④→③→②→① with the correct label expanding at each beat and ← disabling at ①. `arrival` resets `mode`/`promptId`/`temp` (`phases.ts:26-46`, only `taught` has `resetTemp: false`), so the implied phase follows the machine back down; nothing pins the footer forward.

**Finding 2 (Important) — ADDRESSED.** `parseAsPresenterFlag` at `masterclass.tsx:38-44`; wiring at `masterclass.tsx:59` keeps `.withDefault(false).withOptions({ history: "replace" })`. Browser-verified: fresh `?presenter=1` renders the footer at ①; bare `?presenter` works; `?presenter=TRUE` works; `Shift+P` serialises to `presenter=1` (not `=true`). **Finding 3 (Important) — ADDRESSED.** `console-chrome.tsx:54`. Pixel-identical at `sm`+: 640/768/1280px all report height **56px**, `flex-wrap: nowrap`, `padding-top/bottom: 0px`, `padding-left: 24px`, `column-gap: 20px` — i.e. the pre-fix `h-14` geometry exactly (`min-h-14` and `gap-y-2` are inert under `nowrap`).

## New breakage introduced by the fix diff

**1. Important — the disclosure fold is monotone per render but not over time: gates that opened can close again under the presenter's hand.** `index.tsx:193-205`. Because `implied` is derived per render and never written back to `snap.furthest`, returning a control to its default value retracts everything it had unlocked. **2. Minor — folding into the *current* phase lets the footer highlight jump backwards-in-beat.** Same lines. After walking to ④ and stepping back to ①, nudging the dial (visible, since `furthest` is sticky) moves the highlight to ③ and re-enables ←, while the presenter is talking about beat ①. Era I is rebuilt. Seven commits, all local, 113/113 green, typecheck clean, and the whole thing walked in a real browser with measured numbers rather than eyeballs.

## What's on screen now

**The shared link shows everything.** Every control at once — `davinci-002`, both switch cells, both prompt tabs, the dial — no footer, no beats. That's a complete demo for anyone who opens it after the 28th.

**`?presenter=1`, or `Shift+P` live, turns it into your instrument.** A footer appears with four beats as an accordion: only the current one carries its label, the rest collapse to `①②③④` and stay clickable, arrows step and disable at the ends. `autocomplete` → `nobody answers` → `turn the dial` → `2022 · taught to answer`. Arriving at a beat configures the machine and **stops** — nothing ever runs on its own.

**Nothing moves.** The Run button held pixel-stable at `(831, 995)` across ~75 samples spanning idle → streaming → verdict. The status row stayed 56px throughout. The dial arriving at beat ③ produced bounding boxes identical to beat ②. The output panel's height is now reserved rather than minimum, guarded by a test that fails if new copy would overflow it.

**The dial stopped disappearing, and started meaning something.** Rather than retracting it on the flip and calling that an argument, the instruct side got its own per-band answers. Crank to 1.4 in base and it asks *how do I reverse time? who is asking?*. Flip to post-trained at the same 1.4 and it still answers — chattier, with an unsolicited aside about `toReversed()` — but in the shape you asked for. The dice are still there; the format doesn't care. That's the truer claim, and it's the one your seniors will recognise.

## The bug the final review caught, and why it mattered

`dispositionFor` decided what was on screen from the furthest beat visited, and never saw which model or prompt was actually loaded. So: click `a question`, click `post-trained`, press `Shift+P` — and you'd land on beat ① with an unlit `base` nameplate over a post-trained machine. Press Run at the *"it's just autocomplete"* beat and it printed **the ChatGPT-moment verdict**. Your payoff, on the first sentence, in front of the room.

Fixed by `phaseImpliedBy` — a pure function that reads a machine configuration back to the beat that could have produced it — folded into both the beat you're on and the furthest you've reached. Reproduced live before and after.

Also fixed: `?presenter=1` didn't work (nuqs only accepted the literal `true`, so the URL the spec told you to bookmark silently gave you the default view), and the chrome row clipped below 640px — at 390px the dial and the `↺` were 237px off-screen with no way to reach them.

## One thing I did not fix, because it's your call

**Undoing a control retracts what it opened.** Click `post-trained` in default mode, press `Shift+P` — the console correctly opens up — then click `base`, and the post-trained cell, the dial *and* the second tab all vanish while the footer collapses to ①. Three controls disappearing mid-sentence.

It's strictly better than what it replaced, it's one click to recover (tap ④), and it only bites if you toggle into presenter mode *after* using controls. But it's the same class of defect as the Critical above, and it's my fault — I told the fixer "no new state or effects," which is exactly what precludes the correct fix.

The fix is three one-line changes: fold the implied beat into the stored `furthest` inside `handleModeChange`, `handlePromptClick` and `handleTempChange`, so the furthest configuration you ever reached is remembered rather than recomputed. Small, and I'd want the re-walk after it.

Want me to make it? I stopped rather than dispatching a second fix wave, because the process says a residual of this class is yours to rule on, not mine.

## Also logged, deliberately untouched

`isArrowConsumingTarget` lacks the DOM guard its sibling has (unreachable — client-only caller). No `focus-visible` ring on the new tabs and footer (browser default still renders). Collapsed numerals have no accessible name (presenter-only, mouse-only by design). The stream can split the `🦆` for one 18ms frame — I didn't want the streaming hot path touched three days out.

I did **not** run the branch-finishing flow. Nothing is pushed.

content.text:
Both changes are in, `82c8d57`. 113/113 green, typecheck clean, verified in light and dark.

## The tabs

The underline is gone. The active tab now carries the output panel's **exact** fill and touches it with no border between, so the two read as one object; the inactive tab sits on the console's own background and reads as behind it.

One thing that mattered more than it should: `bg-muted` is translucent, so the tab and the panel only composite to the same colour if the fill lives on *each of them* rather than on their shared wrapper. It was on the wrapper, which is why my first attempt still showed a seam.

I also deepened the fill from `bg-muted/40` to full. At 40% the panel was barely distinguishable from the page, so the join — which is now the only thing saying which prompt is loaded — wasn't carrying enough signal for a projector. Screenshots at `.context/era1-iteration/` show before (`1-tabs-before-deepening.png`) and after (`2-tabs-final.png`); `3-dark-mode.png` confirms it holds inverted.
